games.explanation: Cease's strikeout numbers make him look like a problem the Yankees can't solve, but the underlying profile has always been softer than the whiff rate suggests, and this lineup is built to punish exactly that. He runs a walk rate near double digits and gives up hard contact at a rate his ERA keeps papering over, which is a rough combination against a Rice-Grisham top of the order that hunts pitches in the zone against righties. Weathers isn't a star, but he's a lefty in a park where the wind is blowing in and Toronto's damage largely runs through Vladdy, so the run environment favors the road side more than the market wants to admit. At a shade of juice on a coin flip the board should be pricing closer to 57 percent Yankees, you're getting paid to take the better team in the quieter game.

Nobody's going to argue Pittsburgh is the better team, but a plus-233 price on a game the sim sees decided by a fraction of a run is the kind of math the market keeps refusing to do. Skubal is the reason this line exists, and he's earned the reputation, though his splits are noticeably kinder against lefties than the righty-heavy Pirates lineup he'll actually face tonight. Reynolds is the exact power profile that has punished this arm angle before, and a park that inflates homers by roughly a third turns any mistake into a swing of the game. You're getting a live dog in a coin-flippier spot than the board thinks, and +233 is a price worth being wrong at.

Houston is the better team and Hunter Brown is the better pitcher, but the price on the Athletics getting a run and a half assumes a gap that isn't really there tonight. Our sim spits out a 4.5 to 4.5 game, and Jacob Lopez has quietly posted whiff and strikeout numbers that mirror Brown's own, which is not the profile of a guy about to get run out of the building. Brown is excellent against righties but noticeably more hittable against lefties, and Oakland has enough left-handed contact in McNeil and Butler to keep innings alive. A coin-flip game priced like a blowout is where the run line earns its keep, and -108 for the extra cushion is the pitch.

The catch is that Skubal's dominance is a strikeout show, not a slugfest inducer, and games where he racks up whiffs tend to end 4-1, not 9-2. Pittsburgh's pitching staff has been perfectly capable of keeping the Dodgers in a normal-scoring range, and the sim splits these two within a third of a run despite Los Angeles being clearly the better team. Getting a buck and a half at even money in a projected one-run game is the kind of math that doesn't need a hard sell.

Boston is the better team here, nobody's arguing that, but run line prices at Fenway keep pretending underdogs can't hang around for nine innings when the favorite is throwing a fifth starter. The Sox counter Tidwell with a lineup whose top bats are grinders more than crushers, and the park's HR factor plays down in this wind. Meanwhile Devers gets a full night of right-handed pitching he's been punishing to a .391 xwOBA, which is the kind of quiet leverage that keeps a game inside a run.
